# Relational Databases

So far, we've focused on keeping a single spreadsheet tidy. But most real
research projects don't fit neatly into one table — you end up with
several related tables, each describing a different piece of the same
underlying system. This chapter introduces relational databases: a way of
organizing multiple related tables so that a computer, not just you, can
understand how they connect.

## What is a relational database?

A relational database is a collection of interrelated tables. The
relationships between tables represent actual relationships between data
entities — relationships that always exist in real life, no matter how we
choose to store the data, but that only become explicit to the computer
once we structure our data as a relational database.

Consider our frog fieldwork: the first time we capture an individual, we
record its sex and assign it an ID. Every time we recapture that same
individual, we take new biometric measurements. If we stored this in a
single spreadsheet, we'd naturally end up with two tables: one listing
every frog we've ever caught along with its ID and sex, and a second
listing every biometric measurement, with a given frog's ID appearing
multiple times (once per recapture). These two tables are related, because
they both describe the same individuals — but a computer reading them in
has no way of knowing that unless we tell it. A relational database is how
we translate a real-world relationship (these two tables both describe the
same frogs) into a structural relationship the computer can use.

## Why bother with relational databases?

It's fair to ask: if we already know how our tables relate, why bother
formalizing it? A few reasons.

First, designing a relational database forces you to think critically
about the real-life relationships in your data — relationships that are
easy to take for granted, and that many data inconsistencies trace back to
overlooking.

Second, an explicit structure enables quality control that a spreadsheet
can't give you. Imagine adding a table of capture and mortality dates for
each frog, alongside the morphometrics table. It's logically impossible
for any biometric measurement to have been taken before an individual was
first captured, or after it died. In a spreadsheet, a data entry error like
this could sit unnoticed indefinitely. In a relational database, this kind
of impossible relationship can be flagged automatically.

Third, relational databases avoid redundancy. There's no need to repeat a
frog's sex and first-capture date on every single measurement row — as
long as the two tables share the frog's ID, we can always look up and
combine that information on demand. This improves accuracy (nothing to
accidentally enter inconsistently across rows) and saves storage space.

There are further advantages beyond what we'll use directly in this
course: relational databases process large volumes of data extremely
quickly; when stored on an external server, they let every collaborator
work off one centralized, always-current copy of the data, with
permissions controlling who can read versus write; and because computation
happens on the server rather than your own machine, they don't tax your
computer's memory. Understanding relational databases is also foundational
to working with data in many other tools and languages beyond R.

## Database components

The core unit of a relational database is a **table**: rows (records) and
columns (fields). Each row is one observation, and each column is one
variable — the same tidy data principle from Chapter 4 applies here too.

Tables relate to each other through **foreign keys** — a variable shared
between two tables. In our frog example, the frog ID is the foreign key
linking each biometric measurement back to that individual's static
information (sex, first capture date). Foreign keys are what make a
relational database "relational" — a table can have one or more of them,
each linking it to a different related table.

Every table also has a **primary key**: a unique identifier for each
record in that table. Sometimes an existing variable works well as a
primary key — frog ID, for instance, uniquely identifies each row in the
"individual info" table, since each frog appears there only once. But that
same frog ID would *not* work as the primary key for the morphometrics
table, since a frog's ID repeats across every recapture. When no existing
variable is unique enough, we simply add a new column — often just a
serial number — whose only job is to uniquely identify each row.

**Try it now:** Look at this table of frog diet samples:

| diet_item_id | diet_sample_id | frog_id | food_item |
|---------------|------------------|----------|------------|
| 1             | 101              | 3        | fly        |
| 2             | 101              | 3        | ant        |
| 3             | 102              | 7        | beetle     |
| 4             | 103              | 3        | cricket    |

Which column is the **primary key** — the one that uniquely identifies each
row? Which columns are **foreign keys** — columns that link this table to
another table? (Hint: there are two foreign keys here, not just one.) You
don't need to know what the other tables look like yet — just identify
which columns are doing the linking.

## Database design and architecture

A database's structure should mirror the real-world structure of the data
— not whatever happens to be convenient in the moment. Designing a
database is less about software and more about thinking carefully about
how your data entities actually relate to each other.

As a general rule, split tables by **sampling unit**. Data about individual
frogs and data about the ponds they were caught in belong in separate
tables — one has the frog as its unit, the other has the pond — related to
each other through a shared pond ID.

Sometimes two tables deserve to be split even when they share the same
sampling unit. Our frog ID/sex table and our morphometrics table are both,
technically, about individual frogs — but the first holds *static*
information that doesn't change over time, while the second holds
*dynamic*, repeated information collected across multiple visits. Rather
than repeating the static information on every single measurement row,
it's far more efficient to split static and dynamic information into
separate tables, related through the frog ID.

Every column should also hold only **atomic values** — values that can't
be meaningfully divided further. This means splitting a "full name" column
into separate first and last name columns, and never packing a list of
several items into a single cell. Say we're recording frog diet, and each
sample might contain several food items (a fly, an ant, a beetle). If the
diet sample is the unit of our table, we'd end up cramming a list of items
into one "food item" cell — no longer atomic. The fix is to make the food
item itself the unit of the table: one row per item found, with the diet
sample's ID repeated as a foreign key linking each item back to the sample
it came from.

**Try it now:** Imagine a field assistant hands you this table of frog
capture events:

| capture_id | frog_id | site_name    | latitude | longitude | capture_date |
|-------------|----------|---------------|-----------|------------|----------------|
| 1           | 3        | Alder Pond    | 41.7982   | -111.8181  | 2023-05-15     |
| 2           | 7        | Beaver Creek  | 41.8104   | -111.7996  | 2023-05-16     |
| 3           | 12       | Alder Pond    | 41.7982   | -111.8181  | 2023-05-16     |

Using what you just learned about splitting tables by sampling unit: what's
wrong with this table's design? What two tables should this actually be
split into, and what column would link them together? (Hint: think about
what happens if 50 more frogs get caught at Alder Pond — what data ends up
repeated over and over?)

## Data types

Every column in a table has a defined **data type**: the kind of data it's
allowed to hold. Common data types include character strings (text),
numeric values (including special cases like integers), and boolean values
(`TRUE`/`FALSE`). Different database systems recognize slightly different
sets of data types, but these fundamentals are shared across nearly all of
them.

Because each column has a single associated data type, you can't mix types
within the same column — an "age" column, for example, can't contain both
`5` and `"adult"`. If you find yourself wanting to do this, it's usually a
sign the column is trying to represent more than one variable at once (see
"cramming two variables into one column," back in Chapter 4).

## A first look at our practice database

In the next chapter, we'll dive into SQL — the standard language for
working with relational databases — and learn to write queries that
retrieve and manipulate data, as well as build a database from scratch.
The practice database we'll use throughout that chapter (and beyond)
extends our running frog example into a full relational system.

```{r, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
cat('
<div class="mermaid">
erDiagram
  FROGS ||--o{ CAPTURES : "captured in"
  FROGS ||--o{ MORPHOMETRICS : "measured in"
  FROGS ||--o{ DIET : "sampled in"
  FROGS ||--o{ DEPLOYMENTS : "wears"
  CAPTURE_SITES ||--o{ CAPTURES : "location of"
  TAGS ||--o{ DEPLOYMENTS : "assigned in"
  TAGS ||--o{ RAW_GPS_DATA : "recorded by"
  FROGS ||--o{ PROCESSED_GPS_DATA : "tracked in"
  FROGS {
    int frog_id PK
    string sex
    date first_capture_date
    date mortality_date
  }
  CAPTURE_SITES {
    int site_id PK
    string site_name
    float latitude
    float longitude
  }
  CAPTURES {
    int capture_id PK
    int frog_id FK
    int site_id FK
    date capture_date
  }
  MORPHOMETRICS {
    int record_id PK
    int frog_id FK
    date measurement_date
    float weight_g
    float length_mm
  }
  DIET {
    int diet_item_id PK
    int diet_sample_id
    int frog_id FK
    string food_item
  }
  TAGS {
    int tag_id PK
    string tag_model
  }
  DEPLOYMENTS {
    int deployment_id PK
    int frog_id FK
    int tag_id FK
    date deployed_date
    date retrieved_date
  }
  RAW_GPS_DATA {
    int reading_id PK
    int tag_id FK
    datetime timestamp
    float raw_lat
    float raw_lon
  }
  PROCESSED_GPS_DATA {
    int location_id PK
    int frog_id FK
    datetime timestamp
    float lat
    float lon
  }
</div>

<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mermaid@11/dist/mermaid.min.js"></script>
<script>
  mermaid.initialize({ startOnLoad: true });
</script>
')
```

It's made up of 9 tables:

- **frogs**: one row per individual, storing static information (sex,
  first capture date, mortality date if known)
- **capture_sites**: one row per site, storing its name and coordinates
- **captures**: one row per capture event, linking a frog to the site and
  date it was captured
- **morphometrics**: one row per biometric measurement, linked to the frog
  it was taken from
- **diet**: one row per food item found in a diet sample, linked to both
  the sample and the frog
- **tags**: one row per GPS tag deployed in the project
- **deployments**: one row per tag-on-frog deployment period, linking a
  specific frog to a specific tag over a date range
- **raw_gps_data**: one row per raw telemetry reading, as it came off the
  tag, linked to the tag that recorded it
- **processed_gps_data**: one row per cleaned, processed location, linked
  back to the frog it belongs to

Primary keys are unique identifiers within each table (frog ID, site ID,
tag ID, and so on); foreign keys are the shared columns that connect
tables together (a frog ID appearing in the captures table, a tag ID
appearing in the deployments table). The diagram above shows how all nine
tables connect.
